newsitem.title: SPAIN: Westendorp to press for Bosnia war criminal trials.
newsitem.headline: Westendorp to press for Bosnia war criminal trials.

text.p: Western powers will have to resort to pressure if they cannot persuade the main players in the Balkans to hand over indicted war criminals, newly named High Representative for Bosnia Carlos Westendorp said on Thursday.
Westendorp, who takes up his post on June 20, said he would start by trying to persuade the key parties to willingly hand over wanted war criminals.

"Then, you know, there are other arguments. The second (option) is pressure," Westendorp told a news conference in Madrid. "Those who fulfill the commitments will have all our support and those who do not will have no support at all."

Last week, growing international concern that the fragile Bosnian peace process is unravelling led the countries overseeing the Dayton peace accords to issue their toughest ultimatum since the agreement was signed 18 months ago.

The Peace Implementation Council, a body created under Dayton, warned the former warring factions to comply with the peace accords or face sanctions. The United States and its allies threatened to punish anyone "harbouring" indicted war criminals.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright followed that warning with a stern reprimand to the leaders of Bosnia's neighbours Croatia and Serbia, which armed and steered the war efforts of the Bosnian Croats and Serbs respectively.
She demanded they hand over war crimes indictees for trial and stop "stonewalling" on other key aspects of the U.S.-brokered peace accord.

Westendorp said his primary objective would be to seek compliance with the Dayton accords under which Bosnia is supposed to be a single state with two separate entities, one for Serbs and the other a Croat-Moslem federation.

But Bosnia's feuding ethnic factions have resisted integration, many refugees have been prevented from returning home and the inter-ethnic central government has ignored some of the main provisions of the treaty.
"We cannot deviate from Dayton. We must not. That is the only guarantee that the peace is not going to be reversible," Westendorp said.
A NATO-led force in Bosnia is scheduled to leave in June 1998 and there is fear the country could slip back into war after that unless the peace accords are implemented fully.
Resolution of the thorny war criminals issue is critical to maintaining the peace in Bosnia, Westendorp said.
"Coexistence among the communities is not possible unless this issue of the war criminals is solved."
Four years after it was set up by the U.N. Security Council, a war crimes tribunal at The Hague has indicted 75 people. But only nine have been sent to the tribunal to stand trial.
Westendorp, a former Spanish foreign minister, was speaking after meeting his successor Abel Matutes. He said he will make his first trip to Bosnia since his appointment on June 18.
